label: The Dimension of a Variety
notes: This chapter runs from printed pages 477 through 546 and makes the intuitive notion of dimension precise and computable. Several definitions, through Hilbert functions, chains of subvarieties, and transcendence degree, all agree, and Grobner bases turn the count into an effective algorithm.

label: The Hilbert Function
notes: The Hilbert function records the dimension of the space of polynomials of each degree modulo a homogeneous ideal. For large degree it agrees with a polynomial, the Hilbert polynomial, whose degree is the dimension of the variety and whose leading coefficient encodes the degree.

label: Dimension via Leading Terms
notes: Remarkably, the Hilbert function of an ideal equals that of its leading-term ideal, a monomial ideal. So dimension can be read combinatorially from the staircase of standard monomials in a Grobner basis, reducing a subtle invariant to a finite count of exponent patterns.

label: Dimension and Chains
notes: Dimension also equals the length of the longest chain of irreducible subvarieties, matching the Krull dimension of the coordinate ring as a chain of prime ideals. These geometric and ring-theoretic definitions agree, anchoring dimension across the algebra-geometry dictionary.

label: Transcendence Degree
notes: For an irreducible variety the dimension equals the transcendence degree of its function field over the base field, the maximal number of algebraically independent coordinate functions. This links dimension to the number of free parameters a generic point of the variety carries.

label: Tangent Spaces and Smoothness
notes: The tangent space at a point, cut out by the linear parts of the defining equations, has dimension at least that of the variety, with equality at smooth points. Singular points, where it jumps, form a proper subvariety. This completes the core theory. Next: additional Grobner basis algorithms.
